title: Observed impacts of utility-scale photovoltaic plant on local air temperature and energy partitioning in the barren areas
abstract: Rapid progress of solar photovoltaic (PV) technology has caused growing interest in understanding interactions between large scale PV plants and near-surface atmosphere. However few attempts have been made to quantify the impact of PV modules on surface radiative forcing and energy partitioning process. Here, this issue is explored experimentally and analytically in the two adjacent sites located at the PV plant and the natural barren field respectively in Wujiaqu in Xinjiang of China. The results showed that the physical effect of PV panels is not symmetrical in the whole day. During the daytime, compared with the reference site, net shortwave radiative forcing increases 8%, a warming effect on the integrated underlying surface (0.1 K) and a cooling effect (∼-2.6 K) on the ground surface were found in the PV plant. 9.2% of the net radiation (NR) was converted into electric energy (PE), sensible heat flux (H) increased by 30.6% hence resulted in the convection heating effects of 0.64 K and 0.32 K on the near-surface air temperature at the height of 2 m and 10 m respectively, while latent heat flux (LE) and ground surface heat flux (GS) decreased by 49% and 3% respectively related to the reference site. At night, PV panels produce a cooling effect of −0.2 K and −2.3 K on the ground and integrated underlying surface respectively, and less GS is released in the PV plant which contribute to the cooling effects of −0.24 K and −0.08 K on the air temperature at the height of 2 m and 10 m respectively related to the reference site. In the whole day, in the PV plant, H increased by 27.6%, LE and GS decreased by 47.4% and 6.7% respectively, air temperature increased by 0.16 K and 0.1 K at 2 m and 10 m respectively.

## Observed impacts of utility-scale photovoltaic plant on local air temperature and energy partitioning in the barren areas

## **Some of the authors of this publication are also working on these related projects:**

## **Observed impact of utility-scale solar plant on local air temperature**

## **and energy partitioning in the barren areas in summer**

Junxia Jiang[a,b] , Xiaoqing Gao[a,*] Qingquan Lv[c] , Zhenchao Li[a] , Peidu Li[a,b]

_aKey Laboratory of Land Surface Process and Climate Change in Cold and Arid Regions, Northwest Institute of E co-Environment and Resources, Chinese Academy of Sciences,_

_Lanzhou, Gansu 730000, China_

_bUniversity of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, China_

_cLanzhou University, Lanzhou, Gansu 730000, China_

**Abstract:** Rapid progress of solar photovoltaic (PV) technology has caused growing interest in understanding interactions between large scale PV plants and atmosphere. However few attempts have been made to quantify the impact of the PV modules on surface radiative forcing and surface longwave radiation and energy redistribution. Here, this issue is explored experimentally and analytically in the two adjacent sites located at the PV plant and the natural barren field respectively in the Wujiaqu area in Xinjiang of China. The results showed that the biophysical effect of PV panels is not symmetrical through the course of the day. During the daytime the increased net shortwave radiative forcing in the PV plant has a heating effect on the integrated underlying surface and a cooling effect on the ground surface related to the ground surface of the reference site. PV modules decrease the latent heat LE and surface heat flux GS due to the shield and wind resistance, whereas increase the sensible heat H, which resulting in a convection heating effect on the ambient air due to the increased roughness and surface area and low heat capacity. At night the PV panels generate a warming effect on the ground surface and a cooling effect on the integrated underlying surface and the ambient air.

**Key words:** utility-scale photovoltaic plant; land surface process; surface radiation and energy partitioning; _in situ_ observations; barren area

## **1. Introduction**

Excessive consumption of traditional energy has not only accelerated the reduction of fossil fuel reserves and increased greenhouse gas emissions, but also led to global climate change and ecological imbalance, hindering sustainable development[[1, 2]] . The development of envitomentally friendly resources such as renewable energy is considered an effective way to alleviate this problem . Solar energy is considered to be the most promising renewable energy and is expected to play a central role in the global energy transition due to its ubiquitous and predictable nature[[3-5]] . Further, technological advancements, cost reduction and government policy support[[6, 7]] have promoted the unprecedented development of photovoltaics (PV) . In the past ten years, the average annual compound growth rate of the global PV industry has exceeded 35%[[5]] . At the end of 2019, the global cumulative PV installed capacity exceeded 600GW[[8]] and is expected to reach 8519GW

## in 2050[[9]] .

Although PV generation has many advantages,including low emission of CO2 and pollutants, reduce traditional energy consumption and reclaim degraded land[ [10-12]] ,large-scale deployment of solar PV may have negative impacts on ecological functions including soil erosion and compaction, environment degradation[[13-15]] . In particular, space-intensive solar PV infrastructure require a large amount of land[ [13, 16]] . On the one hand, darker-colored PV panels change the radiative forcing on Earth’s surface by reducing the surface albedo[[17, 18]] ,alter the heat transfer between the surface and  atmosphere in the exchange of energy and water fluxes, further regulate the partitioning of available energy into sensible, latent and groud heat fluxes, and ultimately reflected in the indirect impact on the local climate including air temperature[ [19-23]] . On the other hand, large-scale solar PV infrastructure in desert areas usually increase surface roughness[[24]] , which may increase the efficiency of sensible heat transfer from the surface to the atmosphere[ [25, ] 26] . Giving the development rate of PV industry and the changes to the surface properties, resolving the impacts of large-scale PV panels on the regional and local climate is essential.

In the previous studies, most simulations have shown that BIPV can reduce the urban heat island effect, for instance, a cooling effect of 0.01~0.15K was found in Los Angeles, USA when the conversion efficiency of PV panel is more than 25%[[27]] ;some simulations in different cities also showed that BIPV produce cooling effect of 0.2~2.1K during the day and of 0.3~1K at night [28-31] . Moreover, PV panels incorporated in urban pavements are proposed by researchers and can reduce the pavement surface temperature by 5~13K and the ambient temperature by nearly 1K[[32, ] 33].However, due to the complexity of the underlying surface, the albedo disturbance signal caused by the PV panel is also different[[34]] . The simulation in the desert found that the average temperature of the PV area increased by 0.4K[[35]] , and some field observations for utility-scale PV plants in the bareen areas also showed that PV modules increase the ambient air temperature by 2~4K[[36-38]] . A recent study using Modis data showed that the cooling effect of PV plants on the ground surface temperature is 0.81K and 0.24K during the day and night respectively[[39]] . Observed surface parameters such as albedo of the PV plant in Gonghe area of Qinghai China were introduced into the climate model for representing the PV array and the temperature of simulation decreased by 1K and 2K for January and July respectively[[40]] . For the energy partitioning in the PV plant in desert area, the ground surface heat flux decreased while the sensible heat flux increased, resulting the higher temperature at 1.5m during the day[[41]] . Moreover, PV systems may generate a feedback of increased precipitation[[42, 43]] and soil water content, biomass, and plant water utilization rate by reducing evaporation[ [44-46]] .

While the impact of PV infrastructure on some climatic factor was quantified in the above-mentioned studies, it is unclear for external forcing and internal feedback of PV system. The goal of this paper is to advance the understanding the changes in the radiative forcing related to the net shortwave radiation and changes in the surface longwave radiation and energy redistribution as internal feedback mechanisms of PV panels. Given this, we investigate the changes in radiation components above and below the PV panels and energy partitioning introduced by PV modules through the land surface observation of a utility-scale PV plant and an adjacent reference site in the Wujiaqu barren area in Xinjiang of China during the summer of 2020. Meanwhile the present study seeks to explore the nature, dynamics and thermodynamics of atmosphere driven by air-panels-ground interaction and its potential for wind speed and air temperature and provide useful features for characterizing PV panels in the numeric models.

## **2. Experiments and methods**

## 2.1 Site description

This study took place at a utility-scale PV plant in the Wujiaqu barren area in Xinjiang. Wujiaqu is located at the northern foot of the Tianshan mountains and southeast of the Junggar Basin, with a temperate continental climate. It is hot and dry with the highest temperature above 40°C in summer and cold and long with the lowest temperature of 40°C below zero in winter. The area has sufficient sunlight and abundant radiation resources with the annual total solar radiation of about 268.3 KJ/cm[2] and the annual accumulated sunshine hours of 2800~3000 hours, and the annual average precipitation and evaporation are about 150mm and 2000mm respectively.

The PV panels were mounted on the Gobi barren surface about 0.5m above ground-level, with a distance of 1120m from north to south and 1030m from east to west, a coverage area of about 1.15km[2] , and an installed capacity of about 70MW. The azimuth of PV array is south with an inclination of 37 °, the row spacing of PV array is 7.5m, the panel material is polycrystalline silicon, and the maximum power is 250W. The observation site in the PV plant is located at 44.406°N and 87.656°E, with a surface elevation of 439m above sea level, and the reference site (44.409°N,87.667°E, 437m alt) is located 910m northeast of the PV site (Fig 1). The surface of the two sites is Gobi with sparse vegetation and the soil type is sandy soil with good air permeability, but difficult to maintain water and has less nutrients.

Fig. 1. Photos of the monitoring sites for the PV plant (a) and the reference site (c) in the Wujiaqu barren area. The map shows the spatial distribution of the PV plant and the reference site as extracted from Google Earth by the end of 2018 (b).

## 2.2 Study design

The observation towers at the two sites are 11m high, and the observation items mainly include mean field, turbulence field and radiation fluxes as shown in Fig 2 which only . The mean field observations instrument was mainly composed of three layers of wind sensors (Gill WindSonic), air temperature and humidity sensors (Campbell HC2S3), pressure sensors (Vaisla CS106) and were installed at the height of 2 m, 4m, 10 m on the towers in the PV plant and the reference site respectively. The radiometers are all from Holland with type of Kipp&Zonen CNR4 net radiometer, and radiation observations include total solar radiation (DSR), reflected radiation (USR), sky long-wave radiation (DLR) and ground long-wave radiation (ULR). Two layers of radiometers were installed at the height of 1.5m and 10m in the PV plant and the reference site

respectively. Because of the observation tower in the PV plant is located between two rows of PV panels and the field angle of downward sensors is 150°, the diameters for field of view of the downward radiation sensors at the height of 10m above the PV panel and 1.5m below the height of the PV panel are 75.6m and 11.2m, respectively. The observation at the height of 10m can better characterize the PV integrated underlying surface (composed of the upper surface of the PV panels and the bare ground) and at the height of 1.5m can better characterize the radiation balance characteristics of the ground (the ground shaded by the PV panel and the bare ground) in the PV plant. Before the formal observation, A parallel comparison of the radiometers was performed on the flat underlying surface at the height of 10m, to ensure the consistency of results. Turbulence observation instruments integrates an open-circuit infrared gas analyzer and a three-dimensional ultrasonic anemometer with the model of IRGASON-IC-BB produced by Campbell in the United States and are installed at the height of 5.5m and 3m in the PV plant and the reference site respectively, to measure the vertical flux of heat and water vapor in the atmosphere and various pulsations. The sampling frequency of mean field and radiation data is 10 min and the sampling time of turbulence field is 30min. The data used in this paper include 56 days (20 days from 25 June to 14 July, 36 days from 23 July to 27 August) with complete observation from centralized observations in summer and the time used in this paper is Beijing time.

Fig. 2. Schematic diagram of instrumentation in the PV plant, it should be noted that the CNR4 net radiometer at the height of 1.5m and 10m characterize the radiation balance of the ground surface and the integrated underlying surface of the PV plant

## 2.3. Data process

The data quality control was performed before analyzing the observation data to remove wild spots that are obviously unreasonable or caused by instrument failure or bad weather. For example, the short-wave radiation at night is set to zero according to the solar altitude angle; the EC data of the original observations are processed by the EasyFlux online processing software system: mainly including double rotation and plane fitting method coordinate rotation[[47]] , frequency response correction[[48]] , ultrasonic virtual temperature correction[[49]] and WPL correction[[50]] , and finally calculate the 30-minute average sensible heat flux and latent heat flux.

## **3. Results and discussion**

3.1 The attenuation and collection effect on wind and heating effect on near-surface air

The prevailing wind is west and southwest wind (according to the direction of wind blowing) in summer (Fig 3). The wind speed and direction in the PV site all have significant changes at different heights, the frequency of westerly wind increased from 31.8% at 10m to 46% at 2m, and the easterly wind increased from 10.8% at 10m to 20.4% at 2m, while the southerly and northerly winds decreased from 13.5% at 10m to 5.9% at 2m, the wind speed below 2m/s increased from 30.9% at 10m to 69.6% at 2m. Although the wind speed at the reference site also attenuates as the height decreases, its attenuation is lower than that at the PV site and the wind directions at different heights remain almost unchanged. The difference in the distribution of wind speed and direction with height in the PV site is related to the prevailing wind in summer, and on the other hand to the installation height and orientation of the PV panels. The top of the PV panel is about 2.5m above ground-level and placed facing south, impeding the airflow in the north-south direction. When the airflow reaches at the height of 2m, the airflow flowing through the panel is affected by the retardation resulting larger decrease of the wind speed and airflow separation from south and north to west and east.

Fig. 3. Wind roses at different heights for the PV site and REF site during observational period in

summer

Due to the failure of the air temperature and humidity detector at 4m in the PV plant, the air temperature obtained by the eddy covariance system at a height of 5.5m was used in the average vertical profile of air temperature. During the daytime from 9:00 to 20:00, the near-surface air temperature in the PV plant is 0.63°C and 0.29°C higher than the reference site at the height of 1.5m and 10m respectively. One obvious reason is the temperature of PV panels is much higher than the ambient air temperature resulting in the convection heat dissipation to improve the conversion efficiency of PV panels. In addition, compare to the reference site, PV panels increase the surface area and aerodynamic roughness in the PV site, which may generate a higher efficiency of dissipate heat to the near-surface atmosphere through enhance vertical turbulent mixing. This “convection heating effect” can reach a height of more than 10m.

For nocturnal hours, the difference of air temperature between the PV site and the reference site is -0.27°C and -0.1°C at the height of 1.5m and 10m respectively, suggesting that PV panels generate cooling effect for the near surface air temperature due to PV panels have the lower temperature compare to the ambient air and impede long wave radiative cooling of the ground surface at night. The heating effect of PV panels on near-surface air temperature during the daytime is stronger than the cooling effect, hence in the whole averaged diurnally cycle, the PV panels eventually have a heating effect on the near-surface air temperature, making the near-surface air temperature in the PV plant increase by 0.63°C and 0.29°C related to the reference site at the height of 1.5m and 10m respectively.

## 3.2 The effect of PV panels on the ground and the integrated underlying surface

In order to understand the impact of PV panels on temperature of the integrated underlying surface and the ground surface, the average diurnal variations of various of surface temperature was investigated (Fig 4(a)). During the daytime PV panels have a high temperature of up to 55°C as the absorbed solar radiation increase while prevent part of solar radiation reaching the ground and form part of physical shade on the ground, which resulting in the lower temperature of the ground surface but slightly higher temperature of the integrated underlying surface in the PV site compared to the surface temperature in the reference site. On the contrary, after 19:30, the temperature of PV panels decreases rapidly, which was much lower than the surface temperature of the reference site, resulting in the much lower temperature of the integrated underlying surface but slightly higher temperature of the ground surface in the PV site compared to the surface temperature in the reference site, largely caused by the impediment effect of the PV panels to long wave radiative cooling of the ground surface at night in the PV site.

Generally, compared with the surface temperature of the reference site, during the daytime the PV panels have a cooling effect on the ground below (~-1.1°C), and a heating effect on the integrated underlying surface (~1.2°C). For nocturnal hours the difference temperature of the ground surface between the PV site and reference site is slightly (0.04°C) and can be ignored while the temperature of the integrated underlying surface is much lower than the reference site(~-2.5°C)(Fig 4(b)). In the whole day, we found a cooling effect of PV panels on the ground surface and the integrated underlying surface.

Both the impact on air temperature and surface temperature suggest the biophysical effect of PV panels is not symmetrical through the course of the day and the diurnal asymmetry resulted from the following reasons. The first reason is the change of net shortwave radiative forcing induced by the PV panels which only occurs in the daytime; the change of the surface temperature due to the lower heat capacity and physical shading effect of PV panels and energy redistribution near the ground. To further investigate the mechanisms of diurnal asymmetry of PV panels on air

temperature and surface temperature we next present detailed results from radiative forcing and energy partitioning.

3.3 Radiation balance above and below the PV panels

From the above discussion, it can be found that the impact of PV panels on temperature of the near-surface air temperature and surface temperature presents a daily asymmetry, so the radiation components of the two sites at the height of 10m and 1.5m are further investigated for daytime and nighttime respectively. At the height of 10m the daily average cumulative net radiation (NR) of the PV site is higher 1.64MJ/m[2] than the reference site during the daytime. The first reason of the difference comes from the change of the net shortwave radiation as the external forcing item of the system. Due to the lower albedo of PV panels, less shortwave radiation reflected to the atmosphere (USR) in the PV site and the daily average cumulative USR is lower 1.34MJ/m[2 ] than the reference site, correspondingly the net shortwave radiation of PV site (20.47MJ/m[2] ) is significantly higher than the reference site (19.09MJ/m[2] ). The second reason is related to the change of the long-wave radiation as an internal feedback mechanism. Although the ground temperature in the PV site is lower than the reference site during the daytime (Fig. 4) and the emissivity of the upper surface of the PV module (~0.83) is lower than that of the sandy soil (0.94)[[41]] , however the temperature of PV panels is much higher than the surface of the reference site, resulting in a higher temperature of the integrated underlying surface than that of the reference site (Fig. 4), which may cause the upward long-wave radiation (ULR) in the PV site to be higher than the reference site by 0.19MJ/m2. This is contrary to the results of previous studies and may be related to the experimental design, because the reported installation heights of the radiometers were 10m and 3m above the ground for the PV site and the reference site respectively in the literature[[37]] , while in another study the reported heights of the radiometers were 5.7 and 2.8m for the PV site and the reference site respectively[[41]] . With regard to the downward long-wave radiation (DLR), the PV site is 0.44 MJ/m[2] higher than the reference site. The possible explanation is that the high temperature of the PV panel during the day leading to the dry air in the PV site. At night, the negative NR of the PV site is slightly higher (0.04MJ/m[2] ) than the reference site, indicating that the heat release of the integrated underlying surface is less than that of the reference site. Due to the radiative forcing vanish at night, the difference mainly concerns

decreased ULR, which resulted from the lower temperature of PV modules and the integrated underlying surface than the reference site. Over all, the cumulative NR in the PV site is 1.68MJ/m[2] higher than the reference site at 10m during the whole day. The impact of the PV panel on the radiation component is mainly from the reduced USR during the daytime and the longwave radiation response caused by the change of the surface temperature is weak, especially at night.

Fig. 6. Diurnally averaged total radiative fluxes at the height of 10m during the daytime(top), nighttime (second row) and the whole day(bottom) in the PV site and the reference site

As for the radiation components at 1.5m, DSR of the PV site is higher than the reference site during the daytime, possibly because of the refracted solar shortwave radiation by PV panels, while USR in the PV site is lower than 0.7MJ/m[2] of the reference site. The ULR emitted by the ground surface and DLR is decreased by 0.3MJ/m[2 ] and 0.2MJ/m[2] respectively in the PV site mainly because of higher air temperature in the PV site than that of the reference site caused by radiative and convective heat exchange. At night the difference between the PV site and the reference site is minimal. Consequently, for the radiation balance at the height of 1.5m, the net short-wave radiation, while the outgoing long-wave radiation decreases in the PV site increases during the daytime, making the NR 1MJ/m[2] higher than the reference site.

## 3.4 Surface energy partitioning

According to the energy balance equation (formula), the ground surface heat flux is calculated with the assumption that the energy closure is 1 and the energy balance for the PV site and the reference site is showed in the Fig. In the average daily variation, compared with the reference site, the increased of the cumulative sensible heat flux (H) reaches 1.65MJ/m[2] which is equivalent of the increased NR, while the cumulative latent heat flux (LE) and the ground surface heat flux (GS) reduced by 0.59 and 0.36MJ/m[2] respectively in the PV site in the daytime, indicating that the most available energy is released into the ambient air in the form of H through convection. On the contrary, the downward H in the PV site is reduced by 0.09MJ/m[2] compared to the reference site, while LE and GS increase by 0.08 and 0.04MJ/m[2] respectively, indicating that the PV plant has stronger evaporation and the soil releases less heat flux than the reference site. In the course of daily cycle, the H in the PV site increases by 1.57MJ/m[2] , while the LE decreases by 0.5MJ/m[2] compared to the reference site, which is consistent with the previous study[[44]] , the reduced evapotranspiration in the PV site may be caused by the shield and wind resistance of the PV modules.

## **4. Conclusion**

In this study, the measurements of radiation and energy balance below the PV panels and above the PV panels designed for understanding the radiative forcing concerns with net short-wave radiation and consequent surface longwave radiation and energy redistribution of PV plant. We found that the biophysical effect of PV panels presents distinct diurnal asymmetry through the course of the day.

During the day, the increased net shortwave radiative forcing in the PV plant due to the low albedo of PV panels lead to a higher temperature of the integrated underlying surface and the outgoing long wave radiation ULR at 10m increased accordingly as an internal feedback mechanism. While temperature of the ground surface in the PV plant is lower than the reference surface because of the physical shading effect of PV panels and the corresponding ULR decreased by 0.3MJ/m[2] . Part of the increased NR(1.64MJ/m[2] ) in the PV plant is converted into PE(0.95MJ/m[2] ), and the remaining energy is redistributed into H, LE and GS related to the increased roughness and Bowen ratio. The increased H(1.65MJ/m[2] ) is equivalent to the increased NR, while LE and GS is reduced by 0.59 and 0.36MJ/m[2] respectively in the PV site related to the reference site, indicating that most of the energy is released into the atmosphere through heat convection which was caused by the reduced heat capacity and increased surface area and heat transfer coefficient, resulting in the higher air temperature, and the heating effect of PV panels on the near surface atmosphere can reach a height of more than 10m.

For nocturnal hours, the radiative forcing induced by PV panels vanishes, PV panels increase the net longwave of the integrated underlying surface due to the reduced temperature of the integrated

underlying surface while has no impact on the net longwave of the ground surface because of the decreased ULR offset the increased DLR at the height of 1.5m. In the process of energy redistribution, PV panels decrease the H and increase the LE and GS.
